questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, which side is the hypotenuse?
options: The side opposite the right angle
The longest of the two shorter sides
The side next to the angle you are using
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle and is always the longest side. The other two are named relative to whichever acute angle you are working with.

questions.stem: tan θ is defined as:
questions.explanation: SOH CAH TOA: the T stands for tan, opposite over adjacent. Tangent is the only one of the three not involving the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 12 cm and an acute angle of 35°. Find the opposite side.
questions.explanation: Opposite and hypotenuse means sine: sin 35° = opp ÷ 12, so opp = 12 × sin 35° = 6.9 cm. Choosing cosine here would give the adjacent side instead.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has legs 3 cm and 4 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: By Pythagoras, c² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = 5 cm. Answering 25 stops one step early, at the square of the length.

questions.stem: From 45 m away the angle of elevation to the top of a flagpole is 32°. How tall is it?
questions.explanation: The 45 m is adjacent and the height is opposite, so use tan: height = 45 × tan 32° = 28.1 m. An angle of elevation is always measured up from the horizontal.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle the adjacent side is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13. Find the angle.
questions.explanation: Adjacent over hypotenuse is cosine, so cos θ = 5/13 and θ = cos⁻¹(0.3846) = 67.4°. The inverse function takes you from the ratio back to the angle.

questions.stem: Why does every right-angled triangle containing a 62° angle give the same value for tan 62°?
options: Because 62° is close enough to 60° for the values to match
Because the tangent ratio is only defined below 90°
Because every right-angled triangle has the same hypotenuse
They are all similar, so their sides are in the same ratio
questions.explanation: Two angles the same means all three are the same, which makes the triangles similar. Similar triangles have proportional sides, so any ratio of two sides is fixed by the angle alone.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle is enlarged by a scale factor of 4. What happens to the sine of one of its angles?
options: It is a quarter of the size
questions.explanation: Enlarging multiplies every side by 4, so any ratio of two sides divides the 4 out. The angles do not change, and the trigonometric ratios depend only on the angles.

questions.stem: State the sine rule.
options: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
a sin A = b sin B
questions.explanation: Each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same value. Use it when you have a side with its opposite angle, plus one more piece of information.

questions.stem: When should you use the cosine rule rather than the sine rule?
options: Only when the triangle contains a right angle somewhere
Whenever one of the angles in the triangle is obtuse
Given three sides, or two sides and the angle between them
Given two of the angles together with any one of the sides
questions.explanation: The sine rule needs a matched side-and-opposite-angle pair. If you do not have one — three sides, or two sides with the included angle — the cosine rule is the one that works.

questions.stem: State the cosine rule for side a.
questions.explanation: It is Pythagoras with a correction term for the angle. When A = 90°, cos A = 0 and it collapses back to a² = b² + c².

questions.stem: A triangle has sides 7 and 9 with an included angle of 60°. Find the third side.
questions.explanation: Cosine rule: a² = 49 + 81 − 2(7)(9)cos 60° = 130 − 63 = 67, so a = 8.19. With cos 60° = 0.5 the arithmetic stays clean.

questions.stem: State the area rule for a triangle.
questions.explanation: Two sides and the angle between them are enough for the area, without ever finding the perpendicular height. The angle must be the one between the two sides.

questions.stem: Find the area of a triangle with sides 8 and 10 and an included angle of 30°.
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × 8 × 10 × sin 30° = 40 × 0.5 = 20. Since sin 30° is exactly a half, this one needs no calculator.

questions.stem: What is the angle of depression?
options: The angle measured from the vertical
The angle at the bottom of a triangle
The smallest angle in a triangle
The angle measured down from the horizontal
questions.explanation: Both elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal — one up, one down. Drawing the horizontal line into the diagram before you start prevents the usual confusion.

questions.stem: A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of its longest internal diagonal.
questions.explanation: Apply Pythagoras twice: the base diagonal is √(9 + 16) = 5, then the space diagonal is √(25 + 144) = 13. Three-dimensional problems are nearly always two right-angled triangles in sequence.

questions.stem: Which ratio uses the hypotenuse and the adjacent side?
questions.explanation: CAH: cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. Identifying which two sides the question gives you is what chooses the ratio.

questions.stem: sin θ = 0.5 and 0° ≤ θ ≤ 180°. What are the possible values of θ?
questions.explanation: A calculator gives only 30°, but sine is also positive in the second quadrant, and 180° − 30° = 150°. Missing the second solution is the most common error in trigonometric equations.

questions.stem: A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall reaching 4 m up. How far is its foot from the wall?
questions.explanation: Pythagoras with the ladder as the hypotenuse: 25 − 16 = 9, so the distance is 3 m. Finding a shorter side means subtracting, not adding.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side across from the angle you are using is called the:
questions.explanation: Opposite and adjacent swap over if you switch to the other acute angle, which is why you should label them for the specific angle in the question before choosing a ratio.

questions.stem: In a right triangle, which ratio is sine?
questions.explanation: Sine pairs the opposite side with the hypotenuse. Naming the sides relative to the angle you are using is what makes the ratios reliable.

questions.stem: Which ratio is cosine?
questions.explanation: Cosine pairs the adjacent side with the hypotenuse. It differs from sine only in which of the two shorter sides is on top.

questions.stem: A right triangle has hypotenuse 10 and an angle of 30°. How long is the opposite side?
questions.explanation: Use sine: opposite = 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5. The 30-60-90 triangle is worth knowing, because the side opposite 30° is always half the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: Which ratio would you use to find an angle from the opposite and adjacent sides?
questions.explanation: Tangent is opposite over adjacent, so it is the ratio that uses the two shorter sides. Pythagoras finds a length rather than an angle.

questions.stem: In a right triangle the opposite is 7 and the adjacent is 24. What is the angle, to the nearest degree?
questions.explanation: The tangent is 7/24, and the inverse tangent gives about 16°. A small opposite against a large adjacent always means a small angle, which is a useful sanity check.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of sin 45°?
questions.explanation: Half a unit square cut along its diagonal has sides 1, 1 and √2, so sin 45° = 1/√2, which rationalises to √2/2. Exact form means a surd rather than a decimal.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos 60°?
questions.explanation: In a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 2 the side adjacent to 60° is 1, so the ratio is 1/2. The same triangle gives sin 30° = 1/2, which is why the two are often confused.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of tan 60°?
questions.explanation: In the 30-60-90 triangle the side opposite 60° is √3 and the adjacent is 1, so the tangent is √3. Turning it upside down gives tan 30° instead.

questions.stem: When do you use the sine rule rather than the cosine rule?
options: When you have two sides and the angle between them
When you have a matching angle and opposite side
questions.explanation: The sine rule pairs each angle with the side opposite it, so it needs at least one complete pair. Three sides, or two sides with the angle between them, are the cosine rule cases.

questions.stem: A triangle has a = 8, A = 40° and B = 60°. Which rule finds b?
options: Pythagoras, because it is a triangle
The area rule, because an angle is known
The sine rule, because a matching pair is known
The cosine rule, because two angles are known
questions.explanation: The pair a and A is complete, so the sine rule can be set against the pair b and B. Pythagoras only applies to right-angled triangles.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides 5 and 7 with an angle of 60° between them. Which rule finds the third side?
questions.explanation: Two sides with the included angle is exactly the cosine rule case. The sine rule cannot start here, because no angle is paired with its opposite side.

questions.stem: What is the area of a triangle with sides 6 and 8 and a 30° angle between them?
questions.explanation: The area rule is half the product of two sides times the sine of the included angle: 0.5 × 6 × 8 × 0.5 = 12. The angle must be the one between the two sides.

questions.stem: An angle of elevation is measured from:
options: The ground to the object directly
questions.explanation: Both elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal, which is why they are equal between two points looking at each other.

questions.stem: A tree casts a 12 m shadow when the sun is at 35°. How tall is it, to the nearest metre?
questions.explanation: The height is opposite and the shadow is adjacent, so use tangent: height = 12 × tan 35°, which is about 8.4 m. Choosing the wrong ratio gives 17, which is taller than the shadow and should look wrong.

questions.stem: In a right triangle the two legs are 9 and 12. How long is the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: Pythagoras gives 81 + 144 = 225, and the root of that is 15. Forgetting to take the root leaves 225, which is the area-sized answer.

questions.stem: Why does sin 30° equal cos 60°?
options: The two angles are complementary, so the sides swap roles
Both are exactly one half by coincidence
Sine and cosine are always equal
questions.explanation: In a right triangle the two non-right angles add to 90°, and the side opposite one is adjacent to the other. That is why sine of an angle always equals cosine of its complement.

questions.stem: A ladder 5 m long leans at 70° to the ground. How high does it reach?
questions.explanation: The height is opposite the 70° angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse, so use sine: 5 × sin 70° is about 4.7 m. The answer must be less than the ladder length.

questions.stem: Two angles in a triangle are 45° and 65°. What is the third?
questions.explanation: Angles in any triangle add to 180°, so the third is 180 − 110 = 70°. This is often the first step before either trigonometric rule can be used.

questions.stem: A bearing of 135° points in which direction?
questions.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so 135° is halfway between east at 090° and south at 180°. Three-figure bearings are always given with three digits.

questions.stem: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is:
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse sits opposite the right angle, and since that is the largest angle, its side is the longest. Its position on the page is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Why can the sine rule give two possible angles?
options: Because the rule is only approximate
Because sine is the same for an angle and its supplement
Because triangles can be flipped over
questions.explanation: Sine of 40° and sine of 140° are equal, so an inverse sine can point to either. This ambiguous case only arises when finding an angle, never a side.

questions.stem: Which is the adjacent side for the angle marked in a right triangle?
options: The shorter side next to the angle, not the hypotenuse
The side directly across from the angle, never touching it
The longest side, which sits opposite the right angle
Either of the two shorter sides, whichever is drawn lower
questions.explanation: Adjacent means next to the angle, but the hypotenuse is next to it too, so the adjacent is specifically the other one. Labelling all three sides before choosing a ratio prevents most errors.
